To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the one-dimensional representative-agent models may be misleading, and that two-dimensional marketing models may exhibit global phenomena that are not present in their one-dimensional counterparts.

(1) the one-dimensional model for the representative agent may fail to describe the behavior of the system of identical agents; (2) the one-dimensional models may be misleading even in the case of quasi-identical agents.

the dynamics of a representative agent are not always representative of the dynamics of the system of identical interacting agents; the dynamics of the representative agent are representative of the global behavior of the system only when the system is globally stable; and, in the presence of chaotic dynamics, the representative agent is representative of the dynamics in the neighborhood of a chaotic attractor, but not of the global dynamics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of nonlinear discrete-time dynamic marketing models that are based on the assumption that identical agents behave in the same way.

the fallacy of composition in nonlinear dynamic models, and it is intended to be a contribution to a more rigorous analysis of nonlinear marketing models, as well as a contribution to the study of the stability and bifurcation of discrete-time dynamical systems.

the following issues: (i) the fallacies of composition in the modeling of economic phenomena; (ii) the study of local and global stability in nonlinear marketing models; (iii) the application of the results taken from the theory of chaos synchronization to the analysis of nonlinear marketing models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fallacy of composition is present in the nonlinear marketing models considered in this work.
, although identical agents do behave identically, the same is not true for quasi-identical agents.
the one-dimensional representative agent models are not always appropriate to describe the behavior of identical interacting marketing agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nonlinear models of competition, even in the simplest case of a single good, are very difficult to be understood and that the use of the concept of representative agent is not always appropriate.
, when the dynamics of the representative agent are chaotic, the behavior of the whole market may be completely different from that of the representative one.

, when studying nonlinear models in marketing and in economics, the composition of the parts does not necessarily equal the whole, and the study of the dynamics of a representative agent is a necessary but insufficient step for the understanding of the behavior of a whole population of interacting agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, the behavior of identical agents is not the same as that of a representative agent.
, in general, nonlinear models of identical agents are not equivalent to one-dimensional models of a representative agent and, moreover, quasi-identical agents may exhibit very different behaviors.

, in general, the one-dimensional model is not able to describe the behavior of the system of identical agents, and, in particular, the existence of a stable limit cycle in the one-dimensional model does not imply the existence of a limit cycle in the system of identical interacting agents.
